name: Fenoterol
lead: Fenoterol is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist developed in the 1970s as a bronchodilator for asthma and other airway disease, and in some countries as a tocolytic to slow preterm labour [1][2]. It relaxes smooth muscle in the airways by stimulating beta-2 receptors, and is marketed in some regions in inhaled forms, including under the Berotec name [21][25].

In looksmaxxing and body-composition discussion, fenoterol appears as one of the beta-2 agonists, a family that includes clenbuterol and salbutamol, which some people associate with fat loss and lean-mass retention. The interest is based on the role of beta-adrenergic receptors in fat breakdown and heat production, which research has explored for decades [3].

Fenoterol is a prescription medicine where it is approved and is not marketed as a weight-loss product. Its main published literature concerns asthma treatment and a well-known series of New Zealand studies in the 1980s that examined an association between fenoterol inhalers and asthma deaths [4][5].

chain: Increases fat breakdown and energy output in lab and animal work
angle.text: Some community members group fenoterol with other beta-2 agonists as a possible route to fat loss and a leaner look because these receptors take part in fat mobilisation and heat production. It is a prescription bronchodilator and is not used as a weight-loss drug in medicine.

paras: Fenoterol is used as a rescue bronchodilator in asthma and in chronic obstructive airway disease, with onset within minutes when inhaled and effects lasting several hours [1][6][7]. A 1979 crossover trial reported that fenoterol's response exceeded terbutaline's at the doses studied [8], and a 1983 trial compared it with salbutamol by nebulisation [9]. It is also combined with ipratropium in some products [25].
In some European countries it has been used intravenously as a tocolytic to delay preterm birth, though it is associated with more maternal side effects than placebo [1].

Online discussion of fenoterol for appearance centres on fat loss and body recomposition, following the pattern of other beta-2 agonists. Participants discuss it as an alternative to clenbuterol in regions where fenoterol inhalers are easier to obtain. It has no approved cosmetic indication.

Fenoterol binds beta-2 adrenoceptors on airway smooth muscle, triggering a signalling cascade that relaxes the muscle and widens the airways [4]. It is more selective for beta-2 than for beta-1 receptors, though at higher doses effects on the heart can occur [4]. Beta-adrenergic receptors on fat and brown adipose tissue are also part of research into thermogenesis and energy balance [3].

Reviews list the predictable effects of short-acting beta agonists as faster heart rate, tremor and changes in serum potassium and glucose, with tolerance developing on continued exposure [10]. The potential for arrhythmia increases with other heart or lung conditions and with low oxygen [10].

Fenoterol is also known for its link with asthma mortality. Case-control studies in New Zealand covering 1981 to 1983 and 1981 to 1987 reported higher odds of death among people prescribed fenoterol metered-dose inhalers, and a Canadian study reported associations between regular beta-agonist use and death or near-death from asthma [11][12][13][14]. Reviews describe fenoterol-related epidemics of increased asthma mortality in the 1970s and 1980s [2][2]. Fenoterol was withdrawn or restricted in some markets afterward [1].
Where it is marketed, fenoterol is a prescription medicine. Availability differs by country, and it is not sold in several markets [1].

The community material about fenoterol is sparse compared with clenbuterol. Mentions describe it as a related beta-2 agonist available in some countries, with discussion focused on fat-loss claims and on cardiovascular side effects such as raised heart rate and tremor.

Human trials of fenoterol are mainly in asthma and COPD. A randomised double-blind crossover trial in 17 asthma patients compared fenoterol and terbutaline with placebo, finding both increased peak expiratory flow [8]. Other trials compared fenoterol with salbutamol by nebulisation and examined initial treatment of acute asthma, including in children [9][15][16]. A randomised trial in 1990 examined regular inhaled beta-agonist treatment in asthma [17].

Registered trials include studies of Berotec inhalers in asthma, COPD and bronchiectasis exercise capacity, a phase 1 study of fenoterol in heart failure, and a post-marketing surveillance study of 2,914 people with chronic obstructive airway disease [21][22][24][26]. A registered early-phase study compared beta-2 adrenergic stimulation with cold exposure for activating human brown fat [23]. A randomised trial also examined fenoterol excretion during recovery from a weight-loss protocol [18]. No trial has been published testing fenoterol as a fat-loss treatment.

Animal work found that chronic beta-2 agonist treatment can change body composition and protein synthesis in rats [19]. Research on brown adipose tissue has examined beta-adrenoceptors as drug targets for obesity [3].

timeline.event: Clinical reports describe fenoterol (Berotec) in asthma [20].
Controlled crossover trial compares fenoterol with terbutaline [8].
New Zealand case-control study links fenoterol inhalers with asthma deaths [11].
Saskatchewan study reports association between regular beta-agonist use and asthma death and near-death [13].

lore.intro: In body-composition communities fenoterol is mentioned as a relative of clenbuterol and salbutamol.

claims.claim: Beta-2 agonists like fenoterol help with fat loss
claims.believers: Proponents say beta-2 agonists raise fat breakdown and metabolic rate and have been used for leaner physiques.
claims.experts: Studies of beta-adrenoceptors on fat tissue and animal body-composition work exist, but no published trial has tested fenoterol for fat loss [3][19].

claims.claim: Fenoterol is a milder alternative to clenbuterol
claims.believers: Some users say it is shorter acting and easier to obtain in certain countries.
claims.experts: Reviews report dose-related heart-rate, tremor and potassium effects across short-acting beta agonists, and fenoterol is linked to asthma-mortality studies in the 1980s [10][11].

card.summary: A short-acting beta-2 agonist asthma medicine that some people discuss alongside clenbuterol for fat loss and a leaner look.
card.note: Prescription bronchodilator; linked to heart-rate effects and to 1980s asthma-mortality studies.

quick.overview:
Fenoterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used as an inhaled bronchodilator for asthma and, in some countries, to slow preterm labour.

In body-composition circles it is mentioned as a relative of clenbuterol, because beta-2 receptors are involved in fat breakdown and heat production.
quick.mechanism: It stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, relaxing airway muscle; the same receptor family on fat and brown fat tissue is studied in energy balance.
quick.risks: Common effects are faster heartbeat, tremor and lower potassium. New Zealand studies in the 1980s linked fenoterol inhalers to asthma deaths. It is prescription-only where approved.
